content.title: Turn every knob against its slope
content.text: Pill 09 gave every knob a slope: how the loss moves if that knob turns up. The rule that trains the network is one line: new = old − step × slope. Minus, because a negative slope means the loss falls as the knob rises, so up it goes; a positive slope, down. All 2,778 at once. Here is step one, at the random start, with 32 training pictures. The steepest knob is the bias of score 2, slope −0.1173, since seven of the 32 are twos: it moves from 0 to 0.0059. Knob A’s slope on these 32 is only −0.0005; it barely moves. The loss on the 32 pictures: 2.2899 before the step, 2.2570 after. Downhill, a little.

content.title: The step size
content.text: The 0.05 is the step size, the one number of the recipe that nothing learns. A slope is true only near the knob, pill 08’s bowl is not a line, so steps must stay small. Too small and little happens: at 0.005 the loss is still 0.2388 after 60 passes. Ten times larger, 0.05, the run on screen, reaches 0.0416. At 0.5, larger again, 0.0015: faster still. At 2 the knobs overshoot the bottom at every step and never come down: the loss sits around 11 and the network is right 9.9% of the time, chance. Bigger is faster until it is not, and the only way to find the edge is to try.

content.title: A few pictures at a time
content.text: Why 32 pictures and not all 3,823? The slope over all of them is the honest one, but it costs a full pass for a single step. The slope over 32 is a rough estimate that costs a hundredth, cheap enough to take 120 steps per pass over the pictures, and rough is fine: each step is small, and the next batch corrects the last. The loss on each batch jumps around on its way down. After one pass over every picture, one epoch, the average loss has fallen from 2.2916 to 1.2215, and the network already reads 79.1% of the test pictures.

content.title: Watch it fall
content.text: 60 passes, 7,200 steps. The loss on the training pictures: 2.2916 at the start, 1.2215 after one pass, 0.1664 after ten, 0.0416 at the end. The right answers climb the other way: 99.2% of the training pictures, 95.9% of the 1,797 test pictures it never trained on, the number of pill 03. The three pictures of pill 03 along the way: the 3’s score for 3 goes from 8.0% to 99.8%, the 8’s from 8.0% to 99.97%, and the 7’s score for 7 from 11.6% to 0.24%. That one stays wrong, and its loss says so.

content.title: The knobs settle
content.text: Knob A, hidden 6 into score 7, walks from 0.3666 to 1.4176: fast at first, then slower, as its slope shrinks from −0.0199 to −0.0010. Across all 2,778 knobs the mean slope falls from 0.0060 to 0.0011, pill 08’s two fields. That is what trained means: not that every knob reached a bottom, but that the slopes are small enough that further steps barely move anything. Pill 07’s bowl had its bottom for knob A at 2.27; the walk stopped near it, not on it. Sixty passes was the budget.

content.title: What the knobs became
content.text: Nobody wrote a rule for reading digits. A first-row neuron owns 64 weights, one per pixel, so they can be drawn as a picture: gold where a lit pixel pushes the neuron up, purple where it pushes it down. At the start, noise, the random numbers of pill 08. After 7,200 steps, each neuron has settled into a pattern of strokes and gaps that nobody designed: the slopes did it, one small step at a time. Neuron 10, the one of pills 05 to 10, is among them.

content.title: The recipe, complete
content.text: Forward: every value. The loss: one number. Backward: every slope. Step: every knob, a little, against its slope. 7,200 times, and a reader of handwritten digits stands where a random start was. Everything larger is this loop with more knobs and more pictures. Pill 12 puts the standard names on the pieces seen so far. Part 2 builds the engine behind the backward pass by hand, in about a hundred lines.
